scripts.radio: Good evening, and welcome to Kenyans Are Asking. This week, we examine the true cost of public promises. In Mombasa, there is genuine relief: the Sh4.5 billion Makupa Bridge is complete, easing traffic and reconnecting the island's waters. It proves public works can succeed when completed properly. But that progress stands in sharp contrast to the rest of the country. In Kitale, four thousand traders remain stranded in the dust because Masinde Muliro Market has stalled yet again. In Iten, Kamariny Stadium—promised within six months back in 2017—sits abandoned nine years later. And in the national budget, Sh3.7 billion meant for health workers' payroll was quietly reallocated to renovate executive offices. How do we justify plush carpets and fresh paint while our clinics lack medical staff? Meanwhile, citizens pay upfront for electricity and a mandatory housing levy, wondering when those deductions will translate to reliable power and actual homes in their wards. Kwa ufupi: Ingawa daraja la Makupa limekamilika, ahadi za soko la Kitale na uwanja wa Kamariny bado zinasuasua. Zaidi ya hayo, Shilingi bilioni 3.7 za mishahara ya wahudumu wa afya zimepelekwa kukarabati ofisi za serikali. Ni wakati wa kuuliza: je, kodi yako inakufaa wewe, ama inafaa wachache?
scripts.voice_note: Habari zenu. This is the weekly update from Kenyans Are Asking. Look at how our money moved this week. While the Sh4.5 billion Makupa Bridge in Mombasa is finally open, look at what happened to the health sector: Sh3.7 billion meant for health workers' salaries was quietly diverted to renovate executive offices. At the same time, four thousand traders in Kitale are still waiting for the stalled Masinde Muliro Market, and Kamariny Stadium in Iten is now nine years late. We pay our electricity bills upfront, we pay the mandatory housing levy every month, yet everyday services are treated as an afterthought. Let's stop focusing on political speeches and start tracking the budget reallocations. Share this voice note with your neighbourhood group—accountability begins with knowing where the shilling went.
scripts.sms: Usiibiwe: Sh3.7B ya mishahara ya madaktari imeenda kwa ukarabati wa ofisi za wakubwa. Fuatilia bajeti ya kaunti na taifa; kodi yako si ya kupaka ofisi rangi.
scripts.reels: Sh3.7 billion. That is the exact amount quietly stripped from health workers' payroll and moved into executive office renovations. Think about that next time you visit a public hospital and find no doctor or basic supplies. We are told the exchequer is broke, yet there is always money for VIP lounges and executive paint. Priorities are not declared in press briefings; they are decided in budget lines. Who approved this trade-off?
